name: Fruitarian diet
lead: A fruitarian diet is an eating pattern built primarily or entirely on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and without animal products. It is more restrictive than veganism or raw veganism, and practitioners differ on what counts as fruit and whether anything else is allowed.[5] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a route to clear, bright skin and leanness: followers say that removing processed food and animal products and eating water-rich, antioxidant-containing fruit shows up in how their skin and body look.[5]

Published research on the diet is limited to individual case reports. These describe a type 1 diabetes patient who adopted the diet for ideological reasons, a case of reversible dementia attributed to a strictly fruitarian diet, and a leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with long periodic fasts.[1][2][3] No clinical trial has tested a fruitarian diet for skin or appearance outcomes.

Dietitians and health organisations cited in encyclopedic summaries advise against long-term fruit-only eating, citing the risk of deficiencies, particularly vitamin B12, and describe it as unsuitable for children and pregnant or nursing women.[5]

paras: Definitions vary. Some followers eat only plant foods that can be gathered without killing the plant, such as fallen fruit, while others allow legumes, dried fruit, honey, olive oil or cooked foods. Some versions inspired by Jain ethics avoid harming any living thing, including plants.[5]

The diet has older roots in naturopathic and "natural living" movements; the Wikipedia article lists a periodical promoting a fruitarian way of life in the 1896-1918 period and a 1961 book advocating fruit as food and medicine.[5]

Wikipedia describes several variants: some followers eat only plant parts that fall naturally or can be harvested without harming the plant; some avoid grains, seeds or nuts; others include legumes (botanically fruits), dried fruit, honey, olive oil or some cooked foods.[5] The framing as a return to a pre-agrarian gatherer lifestyle is cited as one utopian motive.[5]

Wikipedia lists Steve Jobs as having practised fruitarianism starting in college, and Mahatma Gandhi as reportedly following it for five years before returning to vegetarianism, along with figures such as Arnold Ehret and Dick Gregory who promoted it.[5]

Fruit-centred living has a long line in naturopathic and natural-living movements. The Order of the Golden Age published the journal Herald of the Golden Age from 1896 to 1918, promoting a fruitarian system of living, and Morris Krok's 1961 book Fruit: The Food and Medicine for Man described living on fruit.[5]

A well-known early case is August Engelhardt (1875-1919), a German who joined the Jungborn nudist and vegetarian group in 1899, bought a coconut and banana plantation on Kabakon in German New Guinea in 1902 and promoted a coconut-centred diet he called cocoivorism, drawing a colony that peaked at around 30 members; illness and deaths reduced it, and he died in 1919.[27] Wikipedia also links a 1905 New York Times report on a fruit-based life in the Pacific to Engelhardt's era.[5]

Later followers listed on Wikipedia include Mahatma Gandhi, reported to have followed the diet for five years before returning to vegetarianism during an illness; Steve Jobs, who began practising it as a college freshman; and Dick Gregory and Arnold Ehret, who promoted it in print.[5] Wikipedia notes that Jain-influenced fruitarians pursue ahimsa, avoiding harm to any living thing including plants.[5]

Nutrition sources note that fruit contains no vitamin B12, so long-term fruitarians would typically need supplements, and that protein, calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin D and essential fatty acids may also fall short. High sugar intake raises concerns for people with diabetes and for dental health.[5]

Case literature illustrates reported consequences. A 2021 report described dementia in a person following a strictly fruitarian diet that was reversible after the diet changed.[2] A 2022 report described how a young man with type 1 diabetes switching to a fruitarian diet changed his glucose control.[3] Case reports cannot show cause and effect.

Wikipedia lists possible deficiencies in calcium, protein, iron, zinc, vitamin D, most B vitamins and essential fatty acids, notes that fruit digests quickly so hunger may return soon after eating, and says severe restriction may trigger orthorexia nervosa.[5] It reports that children may experience protein-energy malnutrition, anaemia and poor growth, and that nutritionists advise adults against fruit-only eating for long periods.[5]

A 1978 Nursing Times article discussed the diet from a nursing perspective.[4] A 2023 case report in Medicina described gene-expression findings in a leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with prolonged periodic fasting.[1]

Wikipedia attributes positions to named bodies and writers: Columbia University's Health Promotion Program (2002) lists possible deficiencies in calcium, protein, iron, zinc, vitamin D, most B vitamins and essential fatty acids, and says restrictive eating can bring hunger, cravings, social isolation and a risk of orthorexia; the physician Harriet Hall (2014) describes protein-energy malnutrition and anaemia as risks, especially for children; and the US National Institutes of Health states that natural vitamin B12 comes from animal foods, so strict fruitarians need a supplement.[5] High fruit-sugar intake is also raised as a concern for people with diabetes or prediabetes and for tooth decay.[5] Some fruitarians reportedly use nutritional testing and vitamin injections to manage these risks.[5]

Wikipedia reports that Ashton Kutcher was hospitalised after following a fruitarian diet in preparation for playing Steve Jobs in the film Jobs, and said his pancreas levels were disrupted; the story was widely covered in January 2013.[5][12]

No controlled studies of fruitarian diets for skin, weight or appearance outcomes were found. The literature consists of case reports, including a type 1 diabetes patient whose glucose control changed after switching to the diet, a case of reversible dementia attributed to a strictly fruitarian diet, and a chronic lymphocytic leukemia patient who combined a mostly fruitarian diet with periodic fasting, in which researchers investigated fluctuations in lymphocyte counts.[1][2][3] A 1978 nursing journal piece also discussed the diet.[4]

The idea of eating mainly fruit for clean skin appears in appearance forums as part of a wider interest in detox, raw and plant-only eating. Proponents argue that fruit is water-rich, high in antioxidants and free of processed food. Dietetic sources cited above point to deficiency and sugar considerations.[5]

Discussion on T Nation shows mixed positions. A user describes a relative on an 80:10:10 fruitarian diet whose body 'doesn't respond to exercise' and who does not recover from illness.[9] Another commenter says fruitarian diets can work for endurance athletes eating thousands of calories a day, while a 2012 thread discusses a lifter bench-pressing close to double bodyweight while eating mostly fruit.[10][11] A 2013 thread discusses Ashton Kutcher's hospitalisation after the diet he used to prepare for a role as Steve Jobs.[12]

lore.intro: Fruitarianism is mentioned in appearance communities mainly as an extreme form of clean eating.

claims.claim: Eating only fruit gives clear, glowing skin.
claims.believers: Proponents say that removing processed food, dairy and animal products and eating water-rich fruit leaves skin clearer and brighter.
claims.experts: No published trial has tested this. Nutrition sources describe risks of deficiencies on fruit-only diets.[5]

claims.claim: A fruit-only diet is a safe long-term way to stay lean.
claims.believers: Advocates say fruit is low in fat and calories and that the body is designed to run on it.
claims.experts: Case reports describe nutritional and metabolic problems, including reversible dementia and glucose-control changes in type 1 diabetes.[2][3]

claims.claim: Fruitarianism suits endurance athletes but not strength training
claims.believers: Forum users say fruit-based eating can work for high-volume endurance athletes eating several thousand calories, and some lifters report strength on mostly fruit.[10][11]
claims.experts: No controlled trials of fruitarian diets for performance or body composition were found; the reports are case reports and anecdotes.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: Detox: fruit cleanses the body and skin
claims.believers: Raw-food advocates cite 'detox' as the reason for fruit-heavy eating.[13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's summary lists vitamin B12, protein and other deficiencies instead; no trial has tested skin detox effects.[5]

card.summary: Eating only fruit for clean skin: no appearance trials exist, and case reports describe nutritional problems.
card.note: Fruit contains no vitamin B12; dietitians caution against long-term use.

quick.overview:
A fruitarian diet is based mainly or wholly on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds. Some people in appearance communities try it hoping for clearer skin and leanness.

No clinical trials have tested it for appearance. The published literature consists of case reports.
quick.mechanism: Followers say removing processed foods and animal products and eating water-rich, antioxidant-containing fruit improves skin. This mechanism has not been tested in studies.
quick.risks: Dietitians cite possible shortfalls of vitamin B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc and vitamin D, high sugar load, and unsuitability for children and pregnant or nursing women. Case reports include reversible dementia and altered glucose control in type 1 diabetes.

chain: Eat mostly fresh fruit, water-rich and unprocessed
Lower calorie density, no processed food, more fluid and antioxidants
Claimed clearer skin and a lean frame
angle.text: Followers adopt the diet hoping for glowing skin and low body fat. The claimed route is replacing processed food with water-rich fruit; no controlled study has tested it for skin or appearance.
